RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
Statement 
(a) to (f) There was a break in the progress and intensity of the South-
West Monsoon over many parts of the country during July this year. While 
there was a revival in Andhra Pradesh around the middle of that month, many 
States, particularly, Maharashtra, Gu jarat, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan 
remained in serious deficits till 28th July when the cumulative deficit for the 
country as a whole was —15%. After that date there has been a general 
revival, and the country-wide deficit has come down to -10% on 4th August 
and to — 7% on 11th August. Considerable improvement has occurred in 
some of the above areas. This revival has caused an upsurge in sowing and a 
general improvement of agricultural prospects. As kharif sowing is still in 
progress it will be premature at this state to estimate reduction in kharif 
production. 
Central Government is in touch with the States. The situation is being 
closely and constantly monitored. To enable States to have ready availability of 
funds to deal with any eventuality at the earliest, Rs. 498.77 crores have been 
sanctioned (including Rs. 25.84 crores recommended for Jharkhand) in advance 
from the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) of States with major rainfall deficits in July. 
Based on preliminary reports from these States, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh 
have been allocated 1 lakh and 0.50 lakh MTs of foodgrains respectively to 
initiate relief employment. Railways are transporting water, free of cost, to 
the affected towns in Rajasthan.

†*365. SHRI NARAYAN SINGH KESRI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELAFRE be pleased to state 
(a) whether any special arrangement has been made for rural scheduled 
caste community under National Health Policy; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) if not, whether Government would consider for special arrangement 
for crores of the scheduled caste population in rural areas of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The National Health Policy-2002 gives overriding 
importance to ensuring a more equitable access to health services across the social 
expanse of the country. In order to meet the objective of reducing such inequities 
and imbalances between economic classes and allow the disadvantaged 
section of society a fairer access to pub lic health services, the Policy envisages 
to increase the sectoral outlay in the primary health sector. Further, the Policy 
also emphasises that the state Government will need to design separate 
schemes, wherever required, tailor-m ade to the health  needs of socio-
economically under-served sections of population under the overall umbrella 
of macro-policy prescriptions contained in the National Health Policy, 2002. 
(c) Health is a state subject and State Governments are primarily 
responsible for provision of health care for the citizenry at large including the 
rural scheduled caste population.Government of India is, however, 
implementing the National Health Programmes for control of major 
communicable and non-communicable dis eases like Malaria, TB, Leprosy, 
AIDS, Blindness, Cancer and Mental Health which covers the entire country, 
including the scheduled caste population, both in urban and rural areas. Also, the 
Government proposes to redesign the Universal Health Insurance Scheme 
exclusively for Below Poverty Line (BPL) families and also enhance the 
premium subsidy. The restructured scheme shall largely benefit the scheduled 
caste families as majority of them would be covered under the BPL category.

Statement 
Under the provision of Drugs and Cosmetics Act,. 1940, and rules 
thereunder, the resposibility to grant loan licenses for drugs, rests with the 
Drugs Controllers appointed by the State/UTs Governments. As per the 
feedback available, there are about 4692 loan licences granted in the country for 
manufacture of medicines. 
Under the said rules, it is provided that the Licensing Authority may issue a 
loan licence to an applicant who does not have his arrangements for manufacture 
but who intends to avail himself of the manufacturing facilities owned by 
another licensee. The State Licensing Authority, before grant of a loan licence is 
required to satisfy himself that the principal manufacturing unit has adequate 
equipment, staff and capacity for manufacture on behalf of the applicant firm 
for a loan licence. There is no  distinction between applicant 
company/manufacturing companies in the small, medium or large sectors. 
Information pertaining to details of the licensed companies which have no 
manufacturing base in the country and get their products manufactured on loan 
license and their annual turn over, is not maintained centrally.

†*363. SHRI PYARELAL KHANDEL WAL: Will the Minister of

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) and (b) Public Health initiatives over the years 
have contributed significantly to the progressive improvement of various health 
indicators. These include demographic changes reflected by increased life 
expectancy, reduction in crude birth and death rates and infant mortality rates; 
epidemiological shifts in terms of eradication of small pox and guinea worm, 
containment of number of cases of communicable diseases like malaria and 
leprosy; growth in infrastructure in terms of increase in number of Sub-Centres 
(SCs)/Primary Health Centres (PHCs) /Community Health Centres (CHCs), 
dispensaries, hospitals and beds as also medical personnel including doctors 
and nurses. These improvements show that  the health servi ces created in the 
country have not failed to achieve their goals. 
This various time-bound goals set in the National Health Policy— 2002 
are annexed as Statement (See below). Out of the various goals specified, four 
of them relate to the year 2005. These include eradication

of polio and yaws, elimination of leprosy, establishing an integrated system of 
surveillance, national health accounts and health statistics and increase state sector 
health spending from 5.5% to 7% of the budget. Polio and yaws are on the 
verge of being eradicated and leprosy has reached near elimination level with 17 
States already having achieved it and 7 States close to achieving the same. An 
integrated disease surveillance programme has been launched to cover the 
entire country in a phased manner. A system of national health accounts is in the 
progress of being established. The goal regarding increasing the State sector 
health spending was discussed in the last conference of Central Council of Health 
& Family Welfare held in August, 2003 and States were accordingly 
requested to take apporpriate action on this. 
(c) A three-tier Primary Health Care system consisting of SCs, PHCs

and 3,106 CHCs are currently functioning in the country. An additional 8,669 
new SCs are in the process of being opened during the Tenth Plan based on the 
norms as per the census data of 1991 taking the total number of SCs to 
1,45,980 by 2006-07. The status of health centres varies across States with 
regard to availability of medical and paramedical manpower, medicines and 
consumables and building housing such centres. Presently, there is a shortage of 
around 16%, 19% and 54%, in number of SCs, PHCs and CHCs respectively

also a shortage of around 15% of Auxiliary Nurse Mid-wives in SCs and PHCs 
and 49% in Health Worker (Male) at the Sub-Centre level; the shortage in 
doctors at the PHC level is around 8% wh ere as that of specialists at the CHC

THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) According to the estimates of Maternal 
mortality published by WHO in their publication, "Maternal Mortality-2000"

complications arising from pregnancy and childbirth. According to the same 
report, 136,000 of these are estimated to be in India. However, based on the 
maternal mortality ratios of countries, published in the same report, 42 
countries have maternal mortality ratio higher than that of India. 
Maternal health care is an integr al part of the Family Welfare 
Programme. Certain vertical interventions like the National Nuritional 
Anaemia Control Programme and Tetanus Immunization Programme for 
pregnant mothers have been going on under the Family Welfare Programme 
since 1977-78. In 1992, the nationwide Child Survival and Safe Motherhood 
(CSSM) (1992—97) was launched with World Bank support, for integrating 
various vertical interventions in the area of Maternal and Child Health. 
The ongoing Reproductive and Child Health Programme is being 
implemented in all States/Union Territori es since 1997 and aims at bringing 
down the maternal mortality and morbidity. Under this programme, various 
interventions focused on reducing maternal deaths are being implemented. 
These are essential obstetric care; Emergency Obsetric Care; provision for 
referral transport for pregnant women with complication of pregnancy through 
panchayats; provision of drugs and equipment at first referral units; provision 
of contractual staff like Additional Hea lth Workers, Staff Nurses, Laboratory 
Technicians and hiring of Anesthetists from private sector for provision of 
emergency obstetric care. Funds are also being provided for schemes like 24

health centres; training of dais in all districts of EAG States and selected 
districts in other States where safe delivery rate is less then

Under the existing National Maternity Benefit Scheme, pregnant

better nutrition by providing cash assistance of Rs 500 for the first 2 live 
births. The scheme is being integrated with other ongoing maternal health 
schemes into a new and a more comprehensive scheme called Janani 
Suraksha Yojna with the objective of promoting institutional deliveries and 
nutrition of lactating mothers belonging to BPL families so as to reduce 
maternal, neo-natal and infant mortality. 
The need for bringing down MMR considerably and improving 
maternal health in general has also be en strongly stressed in the National 
Population Policy - 2000. This policy recommends a holistic strategy for 
bringing about total inter-sectoral coodination at the grassroots level and also for 
involving the NGOs, civil society, Pancha yati Raj Institutions and women's 
groups in bringing down Matermal Mortality Ratios and Infant Mortality

Public spending on health in India 
*373.   SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI: 
SHRI DATTA MEGHE: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether according to data available in Human Development Report, 
2004 India ranks 171 out of 175 countries in terms of public spending on 
health; 
(b) if so, whether public spending on health in India is a mere 0.9 per 
cent of GDP; 
(c) whether according to the Planning Commission's latest review, there 
is just one doctor for 1008 people and one bed for 1223 of the population; 
(d) if so, whether there is shortage of more than 42,000 doctors in 
Government run hospitals; and 
(e) the steps Government propose to take to meet the shortage and also 
improve health spending in India? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (e) Although no ranking of countries is given 
for public spending on health in the Human Development Report 2004, based on 
data given in the Report, it is seen that India ranks 171 out of 175 countries in 
terms of public spending on health. According to this Report, the total health 
expenditure as a % of GDP in India is 5.1 % of which 0.9% of GDP is the share 
of public health expenditure in the year 2001. 
Planning Commission has only done an internal review of the health sector 
based on data/information supplied by the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare. As per the statistics worked out by the Medical Council of India, the 
availability of allopathic doctors is at present in the ratio 1:1800. If the 
practitioners of Indian System of Medicine and Homoeopathy are also taken into 
account, the ratio of availability of doctors to the population improves to 1:800. 
Similarly, the population bed ratio (allopathic beds) is 1:1503 i.e. one bed for 
1503 persons as on 1.1.2002. This improves to 1:1124 if all types of beds are 
considered. 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
The Central Government hospitals are manned by doctors from Central 
Health Services (CHS) cadre, which has about 850 vacant posts against a 
sanctioned strength of about 4700 doctors. In so far as hospitals run by the State 
Governments are concerned, norms regarding requirement of doctors have 
been prescribed for Primary Health Centres (PHCs) and Community Health 
Centres (CHCs). As per information available up to March, 2002, there is a 
shortage of 1779 doctors at PHCs vis-a-vis the norms in 8 States across the 
country. However, at the CHC level, shortage of about 7500 specialists have 
been reported by all the State Governments vis-a-vis the norms. In addition, 
there are hospitals at the sub-district/district and the State level. The filling up 
of posts of doctors in such hospitals falls under the purview of State 
Governments and no norms have been prescribed for them by the Centre. 
The Central Government has adopted the policy of downsizing its staff 
strength. Department of Health has taken up the matter for seeking exemption of 
technical/scientific posts of the health sector (which includes all CHS posts) from 
the purview of instructions of Department of Personnel and Training under this 
policy. Assistance is provided to the States for engaging private anaesthetists 
and doctors trained in Medical Termination of Pregnancy techniques on 
contractual basis, to take care of emergency obstetric care and alleviate the 
shortage of trained manpower at the CHC level. Government is making all out 
efforts to increase expenditure on health subejct to sectoral priorities and 
overall budetary resources. External assistance from bilateral and multilateral 
agencies is also mobilised to augment the resources for the health sector. The 
National Common Minimum Programme envisages increasing public 
spending on health to at least 2-3% of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) over 
the next 5 years. The National Health Policy-2002 also envisages inceasing 
public health investment to 2% of GDP by 2010. To achieve this, the Health 
Policy stipulates increasing the expenditure on health by state Governments to 
7% of their budget by 2005 and to 8% of their budget by 2010. The Policy 
further envisages to raise the Central Government's contribution to States 
from 15% to 25% by 2010.

National Surveillance Programme of Communicable Diseases 
*377. SHRI MAM. RAMASWAMY: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) to what extent the National Surveillance Programme of 
Communicable Diseases has been effective not only in controlling and 
preventing communicable diseases but also in helping to forecast the 
outbreak of epidemics; 
(b) the details with reference to some specific instances, State-wise; 
(c) whether the World Bank has extended its support to this 
programme in terms of financial aid and technical and professional expertise; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (d) Na tional Surveillance Programme for 
Communicable Diseases (NSPCD) was launched as a Central Sector Health 
Programme during the year 1997-98 and is operational in 101 districts of all 
States and Union Territories. 
During this period, as part of the programme strategy, multidi-
sciplinary teams called Rapid Response Teams (RRTs) were constituted both at 
the State level and in all the programme districts. The RRTs have trained 
medical & paramedical workers at the di strict and sub-district levels in 
disease surveillance. Existing laboratories  have also been strengthened in all 
the 101 programme districts and in 21 States at the State level. These 
laboratories perform routine laboratory surveillance as well as support 
outbreak investigations, wherever possible. 
The RRTs under NSPCD, apart from performing the routine 
surveillance for communicable diseases, have identified outbreaks early and 
managed them on their own and at the same time prevented and helped reduce 
the mortality and morbidity, thus striving to make the districts and the States self-
reliant in the process. They have also supported investigations of larger 
outbreaks both at the State and national level and even in non-NSPCD districts. 
Currently there are 118 State RRT members and 251 district RRT members 
trained under the programme. During 
46 

[20 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
2003, a total of 199 outbreaks were detected early and managed by the RRTs 
established under NSPCD, details of which are annexed as Statement (See 
below). These included large outbreaks of Leptospirosis and Dengue in Kerala 
and Viral Encephalitis in Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. 
Laboratory support was provided by the NSPCD laboratories in more than 
50% of these outbreaks. 
An Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) is proposed to be 
implemented in the country in a phased manner. The World Bank will provide a 
soft credit of US $ 68 million during 2004—2009 for various activities under 
IDSP. Main components of the project are:— 
(a) To establish an integrated and decentraliszed State-based system for 
surveillance for communicable and non-communicable diseases for 
improving the efficiency of existing surveillance activities; 
(b) Strengthening of public health laboratories for diagnosis of various 
diseases and epidemic investigations; 
(c) Establishment of information technology network for timely data 
transmission and analysis; 
(d) Training of personnel in disease surveillance; and 
(e) Undertaking surveys to assess risk factors for non-communicable 
diseases.

*379. SHRI UDAY PRATAP SINGH: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state:

United States in 1971;

manufacturing this product in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. 
ANBUMANI RAMDOSS): (a) to (c) the drug 'Phenformin' was withdrawn in 
USA in 1971 because of reported occurrence of lactic acidosis in some 
patients with the use of the drug. The matter was also examined in consultation 
with Experts in India during early eighties. It was opined by the Experts that 
lactic acidosis reported in the West is not common in Indian Population and the 
drug was effective as an oral antidiabetic drug. Therefore, the drug was not 
withdrawn or banned in the country. However, the issue concerning 
continued use of Phenformin has been re viewed in light of fact that new and 
better oral anti-diabetic drugs are now available. The matter was then re-
examined by the Drug Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) in its 52nd meeting 
which was held on 10th April, 2003 and after detailed deliberation, DTAB 
recommended withdrawal of Phenformin.

†1786.    SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH: 
DR. MURU MANOHAR JOSHI: 
Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have sent central delegation to the different States 
to assess the effect of drought there; 
(b) if so, the names of the States visited by the said delegation 
alongwith the dates of their visits, separately; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
59 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
(c) the report submitted by the delegation on drought in each of the States; 
(d) the names of the States to whom assistance in form of relief has been 
provided by Government to tackle the problem of drought so far, alongwith 
the nature of the relief provided; and 
(e) the shortfall in the kharif crop estimated to be in each of the States? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE 
(SHRI KANTILAL BHURIA): (a) to (e) During South-West Monsoon 2004, a 
number of States remained in serious deficits till 28th July (1.6.2004 to 
28.7.2004), when the cumulative deficit for the country as a whole was-15%. 
After that date, there has been a general revival and the countrywide deficit 
came down to—10% on 4th August to—7% on 11th August. Considerable 
improvement occurred in many of the above areas. This revival has caused an 
upsurge in sowing and a general improvement of agricultural prospects. As 
kharif sowing is still in progress, it will be premature, at this stage, to estimate 
reduction in kharif production or to identify areas, which show definite signs 
of drought. 
In July, Agriculture Secretary visited Gujarat, Maharashtra and 
Rajasthan for a preliminary assessment of the situation only. Interim demands 
sent by some States need review in view of changed situation, and the States 
concerned have been requested to do so. 
To enable States to have ready availability of funds at the earliest, to deal 
with any untoward eventuality, Rs. 472 .93 crores have been released in 
advance from the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF) to Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, 
Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Punjab, Rajasthan and Uttar 
Pradesh. Rs. 25.84 crores from CRF ha ve been recommended for release in 
advance to Jharkhand. Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh have also been 
allocated 1 lakh and 0.50 lakh MTs of foodgrains respectively to initiate relief 
employment if necessary. Railways are transporting water, free of cost, to the 
affected towns in Rajasthan. 
Central Government is in touch with the States to be prepared for any 
eventuality. The situation is being closely and constantly monitored.

Clean coal technology based fertilizer plants 
1812. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHER JEE: Will the Minister of 
CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a number of power and fertilizer plants in other countries are 
running on clean coal technology/coal gassification process; 
(b) whether eight such plants are under implementation in China alone;

in the country, 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor; 
85 

RAJYA SABHA  . [20 August, 2004] 
(e) whether possibilities of revival of coal based fertilizer plants or 
retrofitting Naphtha based fertilizer plan ts with coal gassification process is 
being looked into; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF CHEMICALS AND FERTILIZERS (SHRI RAM 
VILAS PASWAN): (a) and (b) A number of coal based fertilizer plants are 
operating in other countries and there are four coal based ammonia plants with 
capacities above 1000 tonnes per day under implementation in China. A few 
power plants based on integrated Coal  Gasification Combined Cycle (IGCC) 
technology are also in operation in other countries. The coal gasification 
technology is in the demonstration stage in these countries and is yet to prove as 
a commercially viable option for power generation. There is no specific 
information on the number of power plants under implementation in China 
using this technology. The coal gasification technology is yet to be 
demonstrated for the high ash Indian coals. 
(c) to (f) The Government has not so far received any proposal for setting 
up fertilizer plants based on synthesis gas from coal gassification in the country. 
In the event of synthesis gas from coal gasification being available in adequate 
quantities at economical rates for fertilizer production, the techno-economic 
feasibility of setting up new plants or revival/retrofitting of existing coal and 
naphtha based plants based on this as feedstock would have to be established in 
the light of the fact that indigenous coal has high ash content and its 
beneficiation/washing to bring down ash condent may involve high operational 
costs. In the power sector, pilot coal gasification projects have been established 
at Indian Institute of Chemical Technology and Bharat Heavy Electrical Ltd. 
(BHEL), both at Hyderabad. BHEL has set up 6.2 MW IGCC pilot plant at 
Tiruchi to demonstrate the technology. Efforts are on to set up an IGCC project 
to demonstrate the technology using high ash Indian coal. In this regard an inter 
Ministerial Steering Group under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Power) has 
been constituted for monitoring the implementation of 100 MW IGCC 
demonstration project. This project is proposed to be put up as a joint venfure 
between BHEL and NTPC. Auraiya Gas Power Station of NTPC has been 
selected for setting up this demonstration project.

. THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND

in 9/15 years. A number of Thermal Power Plants have established facilities for collection 
of storage of dry fly ash wherever required. The Bureau of Indian Standards has revised 
its specification for use of fly ash in cement from 25% to 35%. Bureau of Indian 
Standards has also published standards for use of Portland blast furnace slag cement 
which permits use of granulated slag from steel plant up to 75% in the cement 
manufacture. The Indian Road Congress has published the standards for use of fly ash 
in the road construction. A number of State Governments have included fly ash bricks/ 
products/pozzolona cement in their specifications, schedules and tender documents. Fly 
ash utilisation programme of Department of Science and Technology also facilitates 
demonstration projects on manufacture of fly ash bricks and back filling of underground 
coal mines with fly ash. Building Material Technology Promotion Council of Ministry of 
Urban Development conducts awareness programme on use of fly ash bricks/products 
in building construction. Central Government is continuously monitoring the utilisation of 
fly ash and has asked the steel industry to study the back filling of mines with blast 
furnace slag. The State Governments have also constituted monitoring committee to 
monitor the use of fly ash by different sectors.

1856. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed a recent observation of the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India highlighting inter alia that a large 
number of HIV infected patients are not being revealed the actual status of 
their disease which could lead to such persons unknowingly spreading the 
disease among the un-infected persons and the NACO has failed to discharge 
its due obligations in this regard; and 
(b) if so, the details of steps being taken for proper implmentation of the 
HIV/AIDS control programme for timely prevention and treatment of the 
disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) 
HIV testing is being done at voluntary counselling and testing centers and for 
Prevention of Parent to Child Transmission located at antenatal clinics 
established in identified hospitals. Testing is done on voluntary basis after pre 
test counselling and consent of the person is taken before testing. The person 
is called in between 1 to 7 days period to collect the report which is given 
after post test counselling for both HIV positive and HIV negative persons. If 
the HIV positive person do not come to collect the report, the report is not 
sent to the patient as the test is done at the district hospital and medical 
colleges. Moreover, confidentiality of the test result has to be maintained. 
Some hospital counsellor do write to the positive person to report to the 
hospital without revealing the report in the letter. For research purposes 
including surveillance, the testing is being done on unlinked and anonymous 
basis in order to minimise participation and selection bias in sampling. 
Detailed guidelines on Voluntary Counseling and Testing and National Blood 
Policy have been formulated and distributed for implementation under the 
programme.

1876.    SHRI ABANI ROY: 
                            SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA:

state: 
(a) the total number of samples of drugs that have been lifted by drug 
inspectors during the last three years all over the country, year-wise; 
160 

[20 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) the details of percentage of samples declared spurious and the names 
of persons/Licensed companies manufacturing these drugs; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to stop the negative publicity of 
spurious drugs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI PANABAKA LAKSHMI): (a) and (b) As 
per feed back available from Drugs Control Administrations of States UTs, 
38834, 36314 & 40862 drug samples were tested during 2001-02, 2002-03 and 
2003-04, out of which 96,125 and 118 samples respectively were found spurious 
which is 0.25, 0.34 and 0.29 percent of the total samples tested. 
Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and rules thereunder, the 
responsibility for regulating manufacture and sale of drugs including taking 
administrative and legal action against the manufacturers tests with the State 
Governments. Based on the gravity of the offences detected, necessary punitive 
action under the said Act and rules is taken against the manufacturers for such 
categories of drugs by the concerned Drugs Controllers. In view of this, specific 
details of the spurious drugs detected etc. together with their identified 
manufacturers are not maintained centrally. 
(c) In view of the media reports quoting varying figures about the extent 
of circulation of spurious drugs in the country, the Government took a serious 
note of such reports and constituted an expert committee under the 
chairmanship of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar in January, 2003 to undertake a 
comprehensive examination of drug regulatory issues including spurious drugs 
in the country. Based on the recommendations of Dr. R.A. Mashelkar 
Committee, a legislation to amend the penal provisions of Drugs and 
Cosmetics Act, 1940 and to provide for stricter penalties to the offenders 
including a maximum penalty of capital punishment was introduced in the 
Parliament in December, 2003. The said legislation lapsed with the dissolution 
of the Parliament. The steps to introduce the said legislation again have been 
initiated. The salient amendments proposed under the Bill are given below— 
(1) Enhancement punishments relating to spurious or adulterated drugs 
leading to death or grievous hurt within the meaning of Section 320 IPC upto 
punishment of death or imprisonment for a term which 
161 

RAJYA SABHA [20 August, 2004] 
shall not be less than 10 years but which may extend to imprisonment for life and 
shall also be liable to fine or one lakh rupees or upto 3 times the value of the 
goods seized, whichever is higher. 
(2) Penalties for subsequent offences to be enhanced upto 10 years and with 
fine which shall not be less than one lakh rupees. 
(3) Offences relating to spurious or adulterated drugs to be made non-
bailable and cognizable. 
(4) Provision for setting up of special courts to try offences of spurious 
or adulterated drugs. 
(5) To confer powers upon police officers not below the rank of sub-
inspector or other designated officer to institute prosecutions under the said 
Act. 
The proposed amendments will make the law deterrent to the offenders 
involved in the manufacture or sale of spurious drugs. The involvement of 
enforcing agencies like police will help in  speedy investigations to look the 
culprits and in controlling anti-social elements involved in such activities.

Committees on Railway Accidents 
1916. SHRI RAJEEV SHUKLA: Will th e Minister of RAILWAYS be 
pleased to state: . 
(a) whether the recommendations of various Committees including 
Prakash Narain Committee on Railway accidents have since been considered 
and action taken on them; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) and (b) Between 1960 and 1980, three High Powered 
Committees viz. Railway Accidents Committee— 1962 (K unzru Committee), 
Railway Accidents Inquir y Committee— 1968 (Wanchoo Committee) and 
Railway Accidents Enquiry Committee- 1978 (Sikri Committee) went into the 
entire gamut of Railway working and suggested measures for improving the 
Railway Safety. Action for implementation of the accepted recommendations of 
these Committees was taken. 
Thereafter, Railway Safety Review Committee i.e. RSRC (Khanna 
Committee) had been set up in 1998 to, inter alia, review the position of 
accidents on the Indian Railways and to review the implementation of the 
recommendations made by the earlier Committees and to make their own 
recommendations. The Railway Safety Review Committee made a total of 278 
recommendations in both the parts of its report. Of the 242 recommendations, 
which have been accepted fully or partially, 92 have already been 
implemented. Other accepted recommenda tions are at various stages of 
implementation depending upon the availability of resources. 
There was no Prakash Narain Committee on railway accidents. 
However, a National Transportation Safety Board had been set up in 1987 
under the Cabinet Secretariat, with the main objective of bringing about 
improvements in safety in different transport sectors like Railways, Civil 
Aviation, Road Transport etc. This Board was wound up with effect from 1st 
April, 1990. Shri Prakash Narain was the Chairman of National Transportation 
Safety Board. 
After winding up the National Transportation Safety Board, some 
recommendations pertaining to Railways were communicated to the Ministry 
of Railways on which action as warranted was taken.

DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY: 
Will the Minister of RAILWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Railway Protection Force was provided with more powers 
to deal with crimes on trains and railway premises to make rail travel safe; 
(b) whether measures announced in the railway budget have been 
introduced in the railways for curbing offences like sabotage, damage or 
destruction of railway property and hurting people; and 
(c) if so, the what extent  these measures have helped in checking the 
crimes and robberies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RAILWAYS: 
(SHRI R. VELU): (a) Yes, Sir. Railway Protection Force (RPF) has been 
entrusted with the responsibilities for better protection of passengers and passenger 
area (in addition to Railway Property) by the amendments to the Railway 
Protection ForceAct, 1957 and made responsible for minor offences which affect 
the passengers and the Railway System under chapter XV of the Railway Act, 
1989. RPF has taken up escorting of some trains to supplement efforts of the 
Govt. Railway Police (GRP) and also supplement security in many stations, so 
that the GRP (under the State Government) can better focus on serious crimes. 
The task of escorting of trains is being shared by RPF in*co-ordination with the 
Govt. Railway Police to make rail travel safe. 
(b) and (c) The amendments came in to force with e ffect from 1st of 
July, 2004. RPF has taken up escorting of many trains in co-ordination with GRP 
In July 2004 average of 1,288 trains were escorted daily by RPF. While 
escorting, RPF staff keep vigil and prevent crimes. 
However Sections 150, 151 & 152 of the Railways Act 1989, pertaining 
to sabotage and related wrecking of/damage to trains and Railway Properties 
and causing hurt to people etc. are still in the jurisdiction of the Govt. Railway 
Police (GRP) of the States/Union Territory. The investigation and prosecution 
of crime under the Indian Penal Code as well as sabotage related cases under 
the Railways Act, 1989 continue to be with the State Police. 
206 

[20 August, 2004] RAJYA SABHA  
 
 After RPF has started escorting of trains in co-ordination with GRP, 
there has not been any gruesome or sensational case of crime or robbery in the 
train escorted by them. The cases of theft of Luggage, Chain snatching, 
drugging are dealt with promptitude in collaboration with Govt. Railway Police. 
Due to the efforts of RPF, 29 persons for luggage theft and snatching of 
Jewellery and one person for drugging were apprehended. 
The Railways are closely coordinating with the State Governments for 
prevention and detection of cases of violent incidents and take the following 
steps in this regard:— 
(i) Periodical coordination meetings right from the RPF Post-Police 
Station level to the General Manager-Home Secretary level. 
Whenever there is any flare up in the number and nature of incidents, special 
meetings are held for better ground level coordination. 
(ii) RPF has been supplementing th e efforts of the State Government 
Railway Police by deploying additional staff of RPF/RPSF (Railway 
Protection Special Force). 
(iii) RPF has also taken up escorting of trains in crime-effected areas. Such 
crime prone areas have been identified on the basis of reports of 
crime and discussion with State Govt. Police. 
(iv) The Railways has also corresponded with concerned Chief 
Secretaries and Director Generals Police inviting their attention for 
improving the security scenario over the railways. 
(v) Special care has been taken by Railways to provide security to women 
passengers by organizing Women Squads like Surakshini, 
Tejaswani, Durgavahani. Such squads regularly check the women 
compartments to ensure trouble free travel to women passengers. 
(vi) Efforts to institutionalize the sharing of actionable intelligence in crime 
prone States, where the Government Railway Police, RPF officers and 
Intelligence Officers will meet regularly is being pursued.

administrations in tackling violence in  trains and railway premises is 
extended by the Railways.

investing so much money;

programme.

13.5.2004. Similarly, SAIL has also not changed the listed ex-works price of 
steel materials since July, 2004. 
(d) The domestic steel prices have generally moved in tandem with the 
international prices. The rise in demand for steel and the increased prices of 
essential raw materials are the main reasons for the price rise. In the domestic 
market the price rise during August, 2004 can be attributed to increase in Excise 
Duty (8% to 12%) and Service tax (8% to 10%) and the imposition of 
Education Cess (2%). 
In a liberalized environment the Government does not intervene 
directly in the market to influence prices. However, the Government, through 
its policy initiatives, has taken various measures to increase availability and 
stabilize the prices, which inter-alia include:— 
(i) Reduction in customs duty on non alloy steel from 25% to 10%. 
(ii) Reduction in customs duty on alloy steel from 25% to 15%. 
(iii) Abolition of 4% Special Additional Duty (SAD) on imports. 
(iv) Lowering of excise duty on steel items from 16% to 12%. 
(v) Lowering customs duty on several raw materials like coal, coke, 
nickel, refractories, pig iron and sponge iron. 
(vi) Substantial increase in the allocation of steel items, during 2004-05, for 
supply to the SSI units under the existing scheme for supply to SSI 
unit.

27.3.2004 to 12.7.2004.
